catalog_quote: Which syllables are metrically strong and which are weak may be specified either historically or synchronically. Historically, syllables with an original long vowel are strong; those with an original short vowel are weak unless preceded by a weak syllable or word-final, in which cases they are strong. Synchronically, a Mahican syllable is strong (1) if it has a long vowel or (2) if it has a short vowel that is (a) marked diacritically as strong (indicated here by an underlying grave accent), (b) preceded by a weak syllable, or (c) word-final; other short-vowel syllables are weak. Vowels marked diacritically as strong reflect original long vowels that were shortened before |h| (7) and a few original short vowels that have become metrically invariant (e.g., because of initial syllable loss in 4c). sweep_summary: Both stress-titled bibliography hits for Mahican (Pescarini 2018 'Stressed enclitics are not weak pronouns'; Ordóñez & Repetti 2006 'Stressed Enclitics?') are Romance-linguistics chapters that Glottolog attached to Mahican [mjy] by a computational keyword match on 'enclitics' (stated verbatim on both Glottolog reference pages, opened). Neither concerns Mahican; priority none. No new first-hand Mahican stress statement was found or read in this search of works with stress in the title.org and the Carleton OJS Algonquian Papers search, which returns only the two already-held Mahican phonology papers (Goddard 2008/2017 'Notes on Mahican'; Warne 1980). The catalog's deciding source, Goddard 2008 p. 257 (strong/weak syllable rule: long vowels strong; short vowels strong only if diacritically marked, preceded by a weak syllable, or word-final), was re-read in the the text we hold layerendnote 23 lines 2420-2426 citing Pentland 1991:25) and stands unchanged; the only other dedicated treatment, Pentland 1991 'Mahican historical phonology' (in Masthay ed., Schmick's Mahican Dictionary, APS 1991, pp. 15-27), remains print only (archive.org item access-restricted; HathiTrust catalog could not be reached by automated download). Records: and.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and both supporting endnotes are verbatim in the Goddard 2008 text we hold at the stated places (p. 257; endnotes 22/23 on p. 303, scanned-numbered 12/13). (2) Deciding source: a 2008 phonology article by Ives Goddard, the field's authority on Eastern Algonquian, and the sole Glottolog 'phonology' entry for the language; Mahican has had no speakers since the 1930s, so no reference grammar, instrumental study or JIPA illustration exists or can exist; the only alternative (Pentland 1991, 13 pp.) is older, shorter, and is the work Goddard cites for the same rule, and Goddard explicitly notes the Mahican rule treats open and closed short syllables alike (matching our 'heavy = CVV only' coding). (3) list of works to obtain is short: Pentland 1991 (print/controlled-lending only) and the unpublished Swadesh/Michelson field notes; neither is likely to change the weight-sensitiv

tone.quote: There is evidence of three deletion rules. One deleted Proto-Algonquian word-final vowels, an interesting class of exceptions being bisyllabic words containing a lax vowel such as the form for 'land' (no. 37). In initial position Proto-Algonquian *e is dropped. A syncope of Mahican schwa between two non-syllabic elements occurs quite commonly, probably under the influence of stress.
